title: Billy Graham
hookLine: an American evangelist preached to huge crowds worldwide and refused to hold segregated rallies

lines: PEOPLE WALK DOWN TO THE FRONT.
cards: The sermon is over. In a packed stadium, a choir slowly begins an old hymn: "Just as I am, without one plea." And people start to stand up.
One here, a couple there, a man in a work jacket. They make their way down to the front, where the preacher waits. He has invited them, and told them their friends will wait.

The preacher is Billy Graham, an evangelist from North Carolina, and this scene played out in city after city, across many countries. But part of his story isn't about people walking forward. It's about ropes.

teach.b: Graham was a Baptist preacher, and his message was an invitation. In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus says, in the King James Bible: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."
He preached it plainly, then asked people to answer by coming forward.
His hymn for that moment, by Charlotte Elliott, says you don't have to clean yourself up first: you come as you are, and the hymn leaves the rest to God.

teach.h: JUST AS I AM, WITHOUT ONE PLEA.
teach.b: Now the ropes. In the American South of his early years, meetings could be divided by race, with ropes marking where Black listeners could sit.

Accounts of his life say that at one crusade in Tennessee, Graham took the ropes down himself. After that he refused to hold segregated meetings, and he invited Martin Luther King Jr. to pray at one of his crusades.
Some civil rights leaders wished he had gone further, and said so. Both are part of the record. Christians understand coming to faith in different ways.

teach.h: A DECISION, AND A LIFELONG ROAD.
teach.b: Evangelicals like Graham stress a personal decision to follow Christ, a moment you can point to. Other churches stress baptism and a life of growing in faith, sometimes with no single moment to name.
Graham's crusades worked with local churches and sent people back to them. In the hymn, just as I am is about how a person comes to God. Graham's ropes made it about who gets a seat, too.

how: At evangelical revival meetings, the preacher often closes with an invitation to come forward, and counselors from local churches talk and pray with those who do.

games.q: you're Billy Graham, arriving at a crusade in the South where ropes divide the seating by race. what do you do?
o: leave the ropes and preach as planned.
games.why: accounts of his life say he took the ropes down himself, and after that refused to hold segregated meetings.

practice: Think of one person you could invite to something good, a new neighbor, a quiet friend, a cousin you never call: a meal, a walk, a service at your church if that's your world.
When Philip in John's Gospel brought a friend to Jesus, he didn't argue; he said, come and see. Hold them in mind just as they are; if you pray, pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Billy Graham. An American evangelist who invited crowds to come to Christ just as they were, and refused to hold segregated meetings.

orig.note: Greek, in Matthew 11:28: come! — the word behind 'come unto me'.

carryVoice: Your line: just as I am. Looking back: a hiding place, a nun in Paris, Edith Stein, the bells of Nagasaki, plain words on the radio, a table of churches, an open invitation. That's day nine hundred fifty-nine.
